claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn is initially in an FCC state.
The initial alloy has a low dislocation density.
The initial alloy contains intrinsic solute clusters or stacking-fault tetrahedra.
Yield-strength insensitivity to strain rate is driven by athermal dislocation nucleation at pre-existing crystallographic defects.
Thermally activated dislocation glide is not the dominant process controlling yield onset.
The dominant mechanism involves overcoming a high Peierls barrier through local stress concentration rather than thermal assistance.
Solute clusters and stacking-fault tetrahedra act as potent dislocation-nucleation sites.
Applied stress concentration at defect sites triggers dislocation nucleation when the local critical resolved shear stress is reached.
Defect-assisted nucleation bypasses thermal activation and thereby decouples yield strength from strain rate.
Yield strength will remain constant across the tested strain rates at every temperature from 77 K to 600 K.
The activation volume inferred from testing will be near zero or extremely small.
A near-zero or extremely small activation volume would indicate athermal nucleation.
Traditional FCC metals typically exhibit increasing yield strength with strain rate because dislocation glide over obstacles is thermally activated.
The proposed mechanism applies only to single crystals with low initial dislocation density.
The mechanism may fail in polycrystals where grain-boundary sliding or intergranular fracture dominates.
Detecting a significant BCC volume fraction at yield that correlates with strain rate would falsify the proposed athermal-nucleation hypothesis.
An activation volume greater than 100 b^3 would indicate thermal activation and falsify the proposed mechanism.
